title: A prescriptive mathematical theory of deep learning

concept.text: Proposed innovation: a mathematical design theory that starts with explicit assumptions about a class of data distributions and a specified risk, then prescribes a neural-network architecture and training rule with a useful guarantee on performance on unseen data. Its purpose is to turn an explanation of why learning works into guidance that can be used before training. The guarantee would identify the conditions under which the prescription applies, including the loss, available data, finite network size and training procedure.

Proposed scope: the theory should account for feature learning, in which training changes the internal representations used to solve a task, rather than cover only regimes in which those representations barely move. It should connect structured data assumptions to optimization and generalization for finite networks. These are requirements for the intended innovation; the supplied historical paper does not establish the present-day status of those particular theoretical gaps.

The motivating distinction is between a network's ability to memorize and its ability to generalize. Zhang and colleagues showed that tested networks could fit randomized training labels while also generalizing much better when trained on genuine image labels. Unrestricted architectural capacity therefore did not distinguish the two behaviors. Their paper also connected a better explanation of generalization to the possibility of more principled architecture design.

significance.text: The random-label experiments expose a limitation of explaining generalization solely through the size of an unrestricted hypothesis class. Randomizing labels could substantially change generalization without changing the architecture, its size, hyperparameters or optimizer. An adequate explanation must therefore capture relevant distinctions beyond those unchanged properties, potentially including the data and the solutions selected by training. This does not invalidate every capacity bound or every bound containing a parameter-count term.

Conditional significance: achieving the proposed theory would make architecture and training choices mathematically defensible for the distribution classes it covers. A designer could derive a learning system and an associated risk guarantee from stated assumptions, rather than rely entirely on experimental selection. That would be a major advance because the mathematics would prescribe a working design and delimit its expected performance.

Conditional downstream possibilities include reducing unsuccessful training experiments, comparing designs on a common mathematical basis and identifying changes in data that invalidate a guarantee. Certification would apply only to the particular risk and assumptions actually proved. Agreement with empirical predictions would strengthen confidence in the theory's applicability, but would not substitute for a mathematical guarantee. Broader deployment reliability, open-ended language modeling and general intelligence would each require additional results.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed missing capability: a tractable connection from assumptions about structured data to learned representations, successful training and useful finite-sample risk guarantees. The theory would need to explain which features emerge, why the prescribed training process finds suitable solutions, and how performance changes with data quantity and finite network width. These requirements must fit together: a guarantee for an architecture is insufficient if the prescribed training procedure cannot reach the solutions to which it applies.

The historical capacity objection is specific. Because the tested architectures could fit arbitrary randomized labels, bounds based on their unrestricted function classes were uninformative about the much better generalization observed on genuine labels. The paper explicitly allowed that further restrictions could change this conclusion. It also identified implicit regularization—the properties of solutions selected by training—as an area requiring further investigation. The barrier is therefore to identify informative restrictions and mechanisms, rather than to reject capacity analysis categorically.

Proposed scientific and engineering barriers include specifying data models that retain meaningful task structure while remaining mathematically manageable; controlling representation changes beyond nearly fixed-feature regimes; retaining informative guarantees at finite widths and sample sizes; and making prescriptions computationally usable. The assumptions must also be explicit enough to identify when they fail. A theorem confined to an idealized limit or dependent on unknown properties of the desired solution would need a further bridge to become a practical design method.

current_state.text: The supplied historical achievement is the ICLR 2017 work by Chiyuan Zhang, Samy Bengio, Moritz Hardt, Benjamin Recht and Oriol Vinyals, with the reviewed arXiv version revised on 26 February 2017. Its experiments demonstrated that the tested networks could fit randomized training labels, while their performance on genuine image data exhibited substantially better generalization. This established a concrete challenge for explanations based only on unrestricted hypothesis-class capacity; it did not establish that every deep network behaves identically or that all generalization bounds fail.

The paper discussed implicit regularization and the need to understand which properties training imparts to learned models. Its conclusion described the lack, at that time, of a precise formal measure capturing the relevant simplicity of the large models under study. These are historical findings and research directions from the reviewed 2017 work, rather than evidence about what remains unresolved today.

Evidence limitation: the earlier research mentions neural-tangent and mean-field descriptions, empirical scaling laws, sharpness-aware measures and surveys through 2024. The supplied materials contain no corresponding later sources or bounded search results, so those developments cannot be characterized here by date, scope, publication status or demonstrated capability. Likewise, the assertion that no refereed theory met the proposed demonstration by 2026-11-01 is not established by this packet. These omissions leave current coverage unresolved; they do not show that the developments or a qualifying theory are absent.

Access and extraction scope: the supplied review reports that the paper's identity was verified and that retained PDF text extended through page 15 and the appendices without declared truncation. It noted minor extraction defects elsewhere but judged the cited prose passages usable; none of its conclusions depended on visual inspection of figures. The source index also records untruncated HTML and PDF extractions. This record relies on that supplied review, without implying any additional document inspection or contemporary literature search.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: select at least two explicitly defined distribution classes, such as a mathematical image model and a sequence model with a stated grammar. Before experiments, use the theory to prescribe architecture and training choices and predict how test error changes with training-data quantity and finite network width. Fix the experimental ranges, prediction tolerance and statistical uncertainty procedure in advance. A multiplicative tolerance could be used where appropriate, but its value and interpretation would need to be specified prospectively.
completion_criteria.label: Prospectively prescribe architectures and predict errors for two distribution classes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mathematical requirement: provide proofs connecting the stated distribution assumptions and training conditions to the claimed risk guarantees. The guarantees should be informative in the tested finite regimes. For classification error normalized to the interval [0,1], an upper bound at or above 1 would not provide a useful improvement over the trivial bound. Other losses require their own meaningful reference levels; the number 1 is not a universal threshold. A scaling curve selected after seeing the measurements would not satisfy the prospective prediction requirement.
completion_criteria.label: Prove informative finite-regime risk guarantees from stated assumptions and training

completion_criteria.text: Proposed failure and reproducibility tests: predict in advance a specified distribution change that will cause a defined performance failure, then test whether that failure occurs. Publish sufficient assumptions, proofs, implementations, data-generation procedures and experimental details for independent groups to reproduce both successful predictions and the failure case. Repeated runs and a prespecified uncertainty analysis should distinguish systematic agreement from favorable sampling or training variation.
completion_criteria.label: Independently reproduce prospective successes and a predicted distribution-change failure

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: demonstrate that the prescriptions can actually be computed and trained within stated resource limits, and report where the assumptions or guarantees cease to apply. Success on two structured classes would establish demonstrated breadth within those classes. It would neither prove literal universality nor establish coverage of all practical deep networks. These criteria are a proposed evaluation framework, not an established community standard, and empirical success alone would not prove the mathematical guarantees.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate computable, trainable prescriptions with stated resource and applicability limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MAT-03, “A first-principles theory of turbulent transport,” shares the ambition of deriving useful predictions for complex behavior from explicit assumptions. Its subject is physical transport, whereas MAT-07 concerns learning from data. MAT-04, “Proved polynomial-cost solution of high-dimensional nonlinear PDEs,” could overlap when learned methods are used as PDE solvers, but a generalization guarantee does not by itself establish a PDE solver's accuracy or polynomial computational cost.

Roster-based synthesis: MAT-05, “Research-scale machine-checked mathematical discovery,” could help formulate or verify proofs used in a learning theory. Its defining capability concerns mathematical discovery and verification; MAT-07 concerns the content of a particular prescriptive theory. MAT-02, “An effective global Langlands correspondence over number fields,” likewise combines mathematical structure with an effectiveness requirement, but addresses a separate arithmetic problem and would not follow from a theory of deep learning.

Roster-based synthesis: MAT-01, “Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems,” MAT-06, “Classical polynomial-time integer factorization and discrete logarithms,” and MAT-09, “Classical polynomial-time algorithms for cryptographic lattice problems,” concern algorithmic capabilities for specified computational problems. MAT-07 may prescribe efficient learning under distributional assumptions, but that would not establish the broader complexity guarantees sought by those entries. Performance on a structured learning distribution does not settle worst-case computational hardness.

Roster-based synthesis: MAT-08, “Polynomial-time chemical accuracy for molecular electronic structure,” could provide an application setting for learned models. Nevertheless, a learning guarantee would need additional links to the physical target, chemical-accuracy requirement and computational scaling before it could support that breakthrough. MAT-07 remains a distinct advance in mathematical learning theory, overlapping statistics, optimization and computer science rather than subsuming these application and complexity goals.

unresolved_issues: Whether any theory met the proposed demonstration by 2026-11-01 remains unresolved because no contemporary literature review or bounded search record was supplied.
The dates, scope, publication status and limitations of the mentioned neural-tangent, mean-field, scaling-law and sharpness-related developments require their own sources.
The intended distribution classes, loss, architecture families, training rules and resource limits remain to be specified.
Prediction tolerances, uncertainty procedures and the precise distribution-shift failure test remain proposed choices rather than settled criteria.
How assumptions representing real task structure would be verified in an application remains an open design question for this proposal.

brief.title: Mathematical blueprints for learning from data
possible: People building systems that learn from examples could choose a model’s structure and training method before running experiments, with a mathematical guarantee about errors on unseen data. The prescription would start from explicit assumptions about the data and work for models of finite size.
The theory would cover feature learning: how training changes the internal patterns a model uses to solve a task. It would predict how performance changes as the model or its training dataset grows.
why: Designers could spend less time on unsuccessful training experiments and compare designs on a common mathematical basis. Explicit assumptions would also help them identify changes in the data that invalidate a guarantee.

sources.who: Chiyuan Zhang, Samy Bengio, Moritz Hardt, Benjamin Recht and Oriol Vinyals
sources.showed: The tested image models memorized randomly assigned categories yet performed much better on unseen images when trained with genuine categories. Model size alone could not explain the difference.
sources.quote: Deep neural networks easily ﬁt random labels.
sources.cited_for: The distinction between memorizing examples and learning patterns that work on unseen data.
sources.not_established: These experiments do not provide a mathematical prescription for choosing a model and training method.

sources.who: Eshaan Nichani, Alex Damian and Jason D. Lee
sources.showed: They proved that networks can learn internal patterns arranged in a hierarchy. For specified target structures, their theorem bounds the training data and network size needed for low error on unseen data.
sources.quote:
This demonstrates that three-layer networks
indeed perform hierarchical learning.
sources.cited_for: Proofs can connect learned internal patterns, a specified training procedure and performance on unseen data.
sources.not_established: The result depends on particular hierarchical structures and does not establish the full prospective design demonstration.

sources.who: Jason D. Lee, Kazusato Oko, Taiji Suzuki and Denny Wu
sources.showed: For bell-shaped random inputs, they proved that training with reused data can learn polynomial rules—sums of powers of a hidden input direction—with data and runtime requirements close to the theoretical minimum.

sources.cited_for: A specified training rule can achieve strong mathematical guarantees for a structured family of learning tasks.
sources.not_established: The guarantees concern restricted target functions and input distributions, rather than a broadly applicable design theory.

sources.who: Alex Damian, Jason D. Lee and Mahdi Soltanolkotabi
sources.showed: They proved that training can discover the few input directions relevant to certain polynomial tasks. Those learned patterns also support efficient learning of related tasks.

sources.cited_for: Learning useful internal patterns can reduce data requirements and help with related tasks.

sources.who: Spencer Frei, Niladri S. Chatterji and Peter L. Bartlett
sources.showed: For a specified clustered data model, they proved that training strengthens useful internal patterns despite corrupted category labels. Error on unseen data approaches the rate of label corruption.
sources.quote:
We show that, although linear classiﬁers are no better than random guessing for
the distribution we consider, two-layer ReLU networks trained by gradient descent achieve
generalization error close to the label noise rate.
sources.cited_for: Feature learning and useful error guarantees can be proved together even with corrupted training labels.
sources.not_established: The guarantee applies to a particular clustered distribution and training setup, rather than a general prescription.

shown: Nichani and colleagues connected learned internal patterns to mathematical limits on data needs and network size for hierarchical tasks. Damian and colleagues proved that training can find relevant input directions and reuse them across related tasks.

Lee and colleagues proved near-minimal data and runtime requirements for restricted polynomial tasks. Frei and colleagues proved useful error guarantees despite corrupted labels. These are concrete pieces of a design theory, each under specific assumptions.
missing: A unified prescription must connect data assumptions, changing internal patterns, successful training and useful guarantees for finite models.
Predictions made before experiments must hold across distinct structured task families as data quantity and model size change.
Independent groups must reproduce successful predictions and a predicted failure after a specified change in the data.
The prescribed designs must be computable and trainable within stated resource limits, with clear boundaries on their guarantees.

milestones.label: Advance designs and error predictions for two data families
milestones.explanation: The theory would have to prescribe designs and predict errors across data quantities and finite model sizes for two defined data families, with tolerances fixed beforehand. This tests whether it guides choices before training.

milestones.label: Useful proofs for finite models and datasets
milestones.explanation: Proofs would have to connect explicit data assumptions and the prescribed training to useful bounds on unseen-data error at tested model and dataset sizes. This turns predictions into mathematical guarantees.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction of successes and a predicted failure
milestones.explanation: Independent groups would have to reproduce successful predictions and a predefined failure after a specified data change, accounting for variation across runs. This tests reproducibility and the theory’s boundaries.

milestones.label: Usable designs with clear resource and applicability limits
milestones.explanation: The prescriptions would have to be computable and trainable within stated resources, with explicit limits on where assumptions and guarantees apply. This establishes practical use within the demonstrated scope.

uncertain: Whether any theory already meets the complete proposed demonstration remains unresolved.
The task families, error measure, training rules, resource limits and acceptable prediction tolerances remain to be specified.
How to establish that real application data satisfy the mathematical assumptions remains an open question.

page.title: Prescriptive mathematical theory of deep learning
page.definition: From stated assumptions about how the data are generated, a mathematical theory prescribes a deep neural network and its training procedure before training begins. It accounts for feature learning, in which training changes the network’s internal representations, and proves an upper bound on population risk, the expected loss on a new example from the same distribution. Experiments test the theory’s predictions by measuring loss on held-out examples.

goal.need: For one 350-million-parameter language model, choosing training settings on a smaller network cost as much as pretraining the large model once. A perfect training fit gives little guidance about new examples. On CIFAR-10, the same network fit genuine and randomized labels perfectly, yet test accuracy fell from 85.75% to 9.78% when the labels were randomized. Where the data satisfy the theory’s assumptions, teams could choose a network and training settings for a target error and spend less of their computing budget on trial runs.

completion.title: Theory-prescribed deep networks meet proved risk bounds on two data classes in registered, replicated tests.
completion.criterion: For each of at least 2 explicitly defined data-distribution classes of different kinds, such as a hierarchical image model and a sequence model with a stated grammar, a peer-reviewed or machine-checked theorem prescribes a network with at least 3 trained layers, its initialization and a gradient-based training rule, and bounds population risk at finite sample size, width and steps, with features learned in training. Before experiments, the prescription, the predicted test error against sample size and width, and a tolerance are registered. Measured test error is within the bound, which lies below the risk of chance prediction, and within the tolerance; an independent group reproduces this.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas. The two-class, in-advance design test is the Atlas's reading of the design goals stated by NSF and the NSF–Simons collaborations; no outside body has published an acceptance test.
completion.threshold_quote: At present, no framework can robustly predict the observed exponents a priori from dataset and architectural properties across realistic settings
completion.basis: No outside body defines when a design theory of deep learning is complete. Proved feature-learning guarantees exist for single restricted data models, mostly for networks of 2 or 3 layers, and none was registered before the experiments it explains. The test asks for what prescriptive means: a design fixed in advance from the theory, a bound that is informative at the sizes tested, and confirmation by others, on 2 data classes of different kinds so that one tailored model does not suffice. Coverage of natural images or text is not required.

milestones.title: A neural network achieves zero training error on 50,000 randomized CIFAR-10 labels.
milestones.criterion: A trained network interpolates the randomized classification dataset: every training image receives its assigned label. Zhang et al.’s ICLR 2017 experiment meets this test with an Inception network containing 1,649,402 parameters and 50,000 CIFAR-10 training images in 10 classes. Table 1 reports 100.0% training accuracy and 9.78% test accuracy without augmentation or weight decay. This establishes the memorization phenomenon that a generalization theory must distinguish from learning signal.
milestones.set_by: Community convention of interpolation as zero training error; instantiated by Zhang et al., ICLR 2017, Section 1.1 and Table 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: More precisely, when trained on a completely random labeling of the true data, neural networks achieve 0 training error.

milestones.title: A theorem proves gradient descent reaches any positive training-loss tolerance at finite width.
milestones.criterion: For n training examples satisfying stated assumptions, a peer-reviewed or machine-checked theorem specifies a finite network width, initialization and gradient-descent step size. For every ε > 0, it gives a finite iteration bound by which empirical loss is below ε, with stated probability over any random initialization.
milestones.set_by: The finite-width gradient-descent convergence test exemplified by Du and colleagues, ICLR 2019, Theorem 4.1.
milestones.threshold_quote: randomly initialized gradient descent converges to a globally optimal solution at a linear convergence rate for the quadratic loss function.

milestones.title: A proved bound certifies below-chance test error for a trained network with more weights than data.
milestones.criterion: For a trained classifier with more parameters than training examples, evaluate a proved generalization bound numerically at a stated confidence level. Its upper bound on population classification error must be strictly below the error of uniform random guessing, 0.5 for binary classification. A data-dependent bound may use the training sample. For a stochastic network, the certificate applies to error averaged over the stated distribution of weights.
milestones.set_by: Dziugaite and Roy, UAI 2017, distinguish certificates that beat the guessing baseline from bounds that merely fall below one.
milestones.threshold_quote: the bound is nonvacuous, but trivial in the sense that the error rate of guessing is 50%.

milestones.title: A theorem bounds test error for a finite network that learns features under gradient training.
milestones.criterion: For one stated data model and loss, a peer-reviewed or machine-checked theorem specifies a finite architecture, initialization and gradient-based training rule. It bounds population risk at a stated finite sample size, width and number of training steps. The risk proof must use task-relevant features acquired during training. A two-layer network qualifies. A bound proved solely for features fixed at initialization establishes only partial progress.
milestones.set_by: Community convention of a peer-reviewed theorem; the object of study stated by Damian, Lee and Soltanolkotabi, COLT 2022.
milestones.threshold_quote: outside the kernel regime by learning representations that are relevant to the target task

milestones.title: A theorem bounds test error for a gradient-trained network whose depth grows with the data hierarchy.
milestones.criterion: A theorem, peer-reviewed or checked in a proof assistant, shows that a network whose number of trained layers grows with the number of levels L of a stated hierarchical data model, such as a context-free grammar with L levels of composition, reaches a stated population risk when trained by a gradient-based method on input–label pairs, with sample size and training time polynomial in the input dimension. Layer-by-layer training counts. A result limited to 2 or 3 layers, or a calculation without proof, is partial.
milestones.set_by: Ren, Dandi, Krzakala and Lee, 2026, who pose the question for Random Hierarchy Models; community convention of a peer-reviewed theorem.
milestones.threshold_quote: can we prove that deep networks, trained with gradient-based methods and standard input-label pairs, can efficiently exploit hierarchical structure?

milestones.title: A theory fixes a network and training rule in advance and predicts its test error for one data class.
milestones.criterion: For one explicitly defined class of data distributions, a theory is used to fix the architecture, initialization and training rule, and to predict test error as a function of sample size, before the experiments are run; the prediction and its tolerance are registered or published first. Measured test error then falls within the tolerance over the stated range of sample sizes. A proved risk bound is not required at this step. A curve fitted after the measurements, or a setting found by search, does not count.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; the completion test reduced to one data class, without proved bounds or replication. Simon and colleagues name prediction from first principles as the decisive test of a theory of scaling laws.
milestones.threshold_quote: a decisive test of any such theory is its ability to predict these exponents quantitatively from first principles

milestones.title: A theory correctly predicts how excess test loss scales with training-set size in one setting.
milestones.criterion: For a stated data distribution and network training procedure, derive the exponent α for which excess loss scales as n^(−α) in a specified regime, where n is the training-set size and excess loss is measured above a stated limiting loss. Obtain α independently of the measured learning curve. Train finite networks across sample sizes in that regime and show quantitative agreement between the derived exponent and the exponent estimated from held-out losses.
milestones.set_by: Simon and colleagues, Open Direction 7 on predicting scaling exponents from first principles, with experimental tests by Müller and colleagues and by Cagnetta and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: a decisive test of any such theory is its ability to predict these exponents quantitatively from first principles

not_found: No external coverage requirement was found that distinguishes a completed general design theory from the restricted theorems cited here.
No programme, academy or professional society statement was found disputing the value or feasibility of a prescriptive theory for specified data classes.

definition = "From stated assumptions about how the data are generated, a mathematical theory prescribes a deep neural network and its training procedure before training begins. It accounts for feature learning, in which training changes the network\u2019s internal representations, and proves an upper bound on population risk, the expected loss on a new example from the same distribution. Experiments test the theory\u2019s predictions by measuring loss on held-out examples.". Reason: The definition should distinguish the population quantity a theorem bounds from the finite-sample measurement used to test its predictions.

goal.need = "For one 350-million-parameter language model, choosing training settings on a smaller network cost as much as pretraining the large model once. A perfect training fit gives little guidance about new examples. On CIFAR-10, the same network fit genuine and randomized labels perfectly, yet test accuracy fell from 85.75% to 9.78% when the labels were randomized. Where the data satisfy the theory\u2019s assumptions, teams could choose a network and training settings for a target error and spend less of their computing budget on trial runs.". Reason: The CIFAR-10 example shows why training accuracy is insufficient, but the entry omits the cost of choosing training settings and the decision a theory would help teams make.
